summary: Second Peter 2 warns that false teachers will arise among the readers, exploit them, and bring the way of truth into public disgrace. The chapter then recalls examples of judgment and rescue, including angels, Noah, Sodom and Gomorrah, and Lot, before returning to sharp accusations against the teachers. It ends by saying that their promised liberty is actually bondage and that turning back after knowing the way of righteousness leaves them in a worse state.
whyItMatters: This chapter is the letter's central warning against destructive teaching and corrupt conduct. It also shows how the writer holds judgment and rescue together rather than treating the chapter as only a list of punishments.

context.author: The letter names Simon Peter as its speaker; traditional readers accept Petrine authorship, while many modern scholars regard it as a later writing in Peter's name.
context.audience: Believers who already know the teaching the writer wants them to remember; their location is not named.
context.date: Disputed: Petrine authorship places it in the apostolic period, while many critical scholars propose the early second century.
context.setting: A letter-shaped exhortation to believers facing teachers the writer portrays as exploitative, immoral, and deceptive.
context.literaryForm: Exhortation framed as a letter and farewell reminder, with this chapter taking the form of a severe polemical warning.

outline.heading: False teachers and their damage
outline.note: The chapter opens by warning that false teachers will secretly introduce destructive heresies, mislead many, exploit others, and face destruction.

outline.heading: Judgment and rescue remembered
outline.note: The writer recalls angels, the ancient world, Noah, Sodom and Gomorrah, and Lot to conclude that the Lord knows how to deliver the godly and keep the unrighteous for judgment.

outline.heading: Arrogant speech and corrupt conduct
outline.note: The accusation focuses on those who despise authority, speak evil where even angels do not, revel openly, and entice unsettled souls.

outline.heading: The way of Balaam
outline.note: The teachers are compared to Balaam, who loved wrongdoing's wages and was rebuked through a donkey speaking with a man's voice.

outline.heading: Empty promises and worsening bondage
outline.note: The chapter closes with images of waterless wells and storm-driven clouds, then says the teachers promise liberty while being enslaved to corruption and end in a worse condition than before.

keyVerses.text: But false prophets also arose among the people, as false teachers will also be among you, who will secretly bring in destructive heresies, denying even the Master who bought them, bringing on themselves swift destruction.
keyVerses.why: This first verse names the danger that controls the whole chapter: false teachers inside the community and the destructive effect of their teaching.

keyVerses.text: then the Lord knows how to deliver the godly out of temptation and to keep the unrighteous under punishment for the day of judgment,
keyVerses.why: This is the conclusion drawn from the examples of angels, Noah, Sodom and Gomorrah, and Lot. It keeps rescue and judgment together.

keyVerses.text: promising them liberty, while they themselves are bondservants of corruption; for a man is brought into bondage by whoever overcomes him.
keyVerses.why: This verse exposes the contradiction the writer sees in the teachers: they offer freedom while being ruled by corruption.

keyVerses.text: For it would be better for them not to have known the way of righteousness, than after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them.
keyVerses.why: This gives the chapter's final warning its weight: turning back after knowing the way of righteousness is treated as especially serious.

questions.question: Who are the false teachers in this chapter?
questions.answer: The chapter does not give their names, location, or their own account of what they taught. It gives the writer's accusations: they bring destructive heresies, deny the Master, exploit people with deceptive words, and promote conduct he calls immoral and corrupt.

questions.question: What are "destructive heresies"?
questions.answer: In this verse, the phrase refers to teachings the writer says damage the community and lead toward destruction. He connects the warning with denying the Master, immoral conduct, greed, exploitation, and deceptive words. The chapter gives these accusations without spelling out the teachers' complete beliefs or a formal creed.

questions.question: Why does the chapter mention angels, Noah, Sodom and Gomorrah, and Lot?
questions.answer: These examples form one long argument from verses 4-9. The writer uses them to say that God did not ignore wrongdoing, but also preserved Noah and delivered Lot. The point is not only punishment; verse 9 says the Lord knows how to deliver the godly and keep the unrighteous for judgment.

questions.question: What is Tartarus?
questions.answer: Tartarus is a term from Greek mythology for a place of confinement and punishment. Here it describes the confinement of sinning angels awaiting judgment; using the term does not import a complete mythological system into the chapter. WEB keeps the name Tartarus where KJV uses hell. WEB also has pits of darkness, while KJV and the SBL Greek comparison text have chains, reflecting a different textual reading.

questions.question: Does verse 9 mean the godly never suffer temptation?
questions.answer: No. The verse says the Lord knows how to deliver the godly out of temptation, not that they never face it. The examples of Noah and Lot show danger and distress before rescue.

questions.question: Why is the language against the teachers so severe?
questions.answer: The chapter is a polemical warning, so it uses strong images and accusations: unreasoning creatures, spots and defects, wells without water, and clouds driven by a storm. Readers should notice that these are the writer's judgments about opponents, not a neutral report from both sides of a dispute.

questions.question: Who is Balaam, and why is he used here?
questions.answer: The chapter identifies him as Balaam the son of Beor and says he loved the wages of wrongdoing. It recalls his rebuke through a speechless donkey to illustrate disobedience checked by an unexpected voice. The point in this chapter is the comparison between the teachers' greed and Balaam's way.

questions.question: How can people promise liberty and still be bondservants?
questions.answer: Verse 19 says the teachers promise liberty while they themselves are bondservants of corruption. The explanation follows in the same verse: a person is brought into bondage by whoever overcomes him. The chapter is warning that a message advertised as freedom can still leave people ruled by destructive desires.

questions.question: Do verses 20-22 settle every debate about falling away from salvation?
questions.answer: The passage warns that if people escape the world's defilement through knowledge of Jesus Christ and then become entangled again, their last condition is worse than their first. The images of a returning dog and a washed sow make that reversal vivid. Interpreters differ over how this warning relates to wider doctrines of salvation and perseverance; its immediate force is the seriousness of returning to corruption after knowing the way of righteousness.

glossary.def: People the writer says will arise among the readers and secretly bring in destructive teaching.
The term used in verse 4 for where sinning angels are cast and reserved for judgment.
A figure recalled in verses 15-16 as one who loved the wages of wrongdoing and was rebuked for disobedience.
The freedom promised by the teachers in verse 19, which the writer contrasts with bondage to corruption.

reviewer: Codex editorial panel (2 Peter, Titus, Nahum)
